title: 可编程光子计算：从器件物理到AI加速与光互连
abstract: Large-scale photonic computing is transitioning from isolated proof-of-concept devices toward co-designed system architectures; its path to sustained advantage over electronics depends not on any single breakthrough but on the joint maturation of material platforms, programmable mesh scalability mechanisms, and electronic-photonic co-integration strategies across AI acceleration and optical interconnect domains. The field has demonstrated compelling per-operation energy efficiency and bandwidth density for specific photonic primitives---matrix multiplication, wavelength routing, and coherent detection---but system-level throughput, reconfigurability, and total cost of ownership remain constrained by cascaded loss, thermal crosstalk, control overhead, and the absence of standardized benchmarking. This review argues that progress will be determined by architectures that treat photonic hardware as a co-designed substrate: one where material choices (silicon photonics versus thin-film lithium niobate) are matched to workload characteristics (inference versus training, dense versus sparse), where programmable mesh topologies are optimized for algorithmic structure rather than generic connectivity, and where the electronic control plane is minimized through intelligent mapping and calibration protocols. Optical interconnects represent the nearer-term value proposition because they inherit telecom-grade reliability and scale with existing fiber infrastructure, whereas photonic AI accelerators demand novel co-design between algorithms and hardware. The synthesis across these domains reveals a common scaling bottleneck---loss accumulation and calibration complexity in large meshes---that both interconnect fabrics and computational accelerators must address through architectural innovation rather than component improvement alone.
